bracketStart.s: IRS, Revenue Procedure 2022-38 (inflation-adjusted items for tax year 2023), Section 3.01 Tax Rate Tables
bracketStart.use: The engine uses the MARRIED-FILING-JOINTLY threshold. SOI Table 3.5 is all returns with filing statuses combined (the by-status table is 3.4), so one threshold has to be chosen; joint returns dominate the AGI classes above $1 million. Using the unmarried threshold instead would subtract about $115,000 more per return, lowering the computed base slightly.

eti.sSSG: Saez, Slemrod & Giertz, JEL 2012 — "the best available estimates range from 0.12 to 0.40"; the authors add "there are no truly convincing estimates of the long-run elasticity."
eti.sDS: Diamond & Saez, JEP 2011 — 0.57 on the current taxable-income base vs 0.17 on a broad base.
eti.coupling: Saez/Slemrod/Giertz: "the ETI can be thought of as a policy choice." Diamond & Saez: the avoidance component "is not an immutable parameter and can be reduced through base broadening and tax enforcement."
eti.notLabor: DO NOT describe ETI as a labor-supply elasticity in the why-panel. It is a REPORTED-INCOME elasticity, and at the top it mostly reflects avoidance and income-shifting, not real output changes.

tauStar.label: 73% IS AN ALL-IN COMBINED RATE — federal income + state + payroll + sales. The authors' own comparison baseline is a 42.5% combined US top rate. If the tool shows 73% next to a federal statutory bracket it WILL mislead. Label it every time.
tauStar.s: Diamond & Saez, JEP 2011, tau* = 1/(1 + a*e), a = 1.5
tauStar.critiqueSrc: Badel, Huggett & Luo, Economic Journal 2020 — approximately 49% in their human-capital model
tauStar.neverClaim: The revenue-maximizing rate is NOT the optimal rate. Optimality is an ethical judgment about how much we should value a dollar to a rich person versus a poor one; revenue maximization is an empirical question. Conflating them is on the never-claim list.

cg.sPersistent: Dowd, McClelland & Muthitacharoen, National Tax Journal 68(3) 2015 — preferred persistent elasticity -0.72. (Cite the 2015 NTJ version, not the CBO working paper, which says -0.79.)
cg.sLow: Agersnap & Zidar, NBER w27705 (2020) — ten-year revenue elasticity of -0.5 to -0.3; long-run revenue-maximizing rates of 38-47%. This is a REVENUE elasticity, not a realizations elasticity, and is not directly comparable to -0.72 without conversion.
cg.stepUpMech: additional base-broadening reforms, like eliminating stepped-up basis and making charitable giving a realization event, will decrease the elasticity of the tax base to rate changes.

rejects.s: Ramey & Zubairy, Government Spending Multipliers in Good Times and in Bad: Evidence from US Historical Data, Journal of Political Economy 126(2), 2018, pp. 850-901
rejects.q: multipliers "below unity irrespective of the amount of slack in the economy"

mult.resolution: The ZLB half of the claim survives partially (Ramey-Zubairy concede 'more mixed' at the ZLB, with some specifications reaching 1.5). The recession/slack half is DIRECTLY CONTRADICTED. The 'recession vs normal' regime dial must carry a visible note that the profession is split.

mpc.sJP: Jappelli & Pistaferri, AEJ: Macro 2014 — 65% at the lowest cash-on-hand percentile falling to 30% for the richest, 48% on average. ITALIAN survey data on HYPOTHETICAL responses.
mpc.sFed: Fisher et al., Boston Fed WP 19-4 — the authors flag their own estimates as "at the low end of the range examined in other research." Quintiles are by WEALTH, which does not map cleanly onto income.
mpc.verdict: THE QUALITATIVE GRADIENT IS ROBUST ACROSS SOURCES; THE SPECIFIC NUMBERS ARE NOT. The dossier's 0.5-0.9 low-income band is unsupported — 0.65 is the verified top of the low-liquidity range. Ship as a gradient with wide, visible bounds, never as two point values. Note also that the Boston Fed quintiles are by WEALTH, which does not map cleanly onto income.

incidence.headline: THE WIDEST DISAGREEMENT IN THIS ENTIRE DATASET — 18% (Treasury) to 70%+ (Tax Foundation), a ~4x range on a first-order parameter. That spread IS the honest headline for this dial.

shops.caveat: This is a LONG-RUN assumption with a phase-in: 'a provision enacted in the first year of the ten-year budget window reaches a long-run equilibrium in the final year of the 10-year budget window.' The 25/75 split is NOT the incidence in year 1. This matters for any year-by-year display.

The 82% decomposes into 63% SUPERNORMAL return and 18% normal return. The supernormal share is doing most of the work, and that decomposition is the substantive methodological claim, not the headline split. A dial that slides labor share from 18% to 70% is implicitly sliding an assumption about how much corporate income is economic rent — the why-panel should say so.
TPC uses a DIFFERENT split for timing changes: 'borne 50 percent by labor and 50 percent by all capital.' JCT and CBO do not make this distinction.

An advocacy organization's synthesis of a selected literature, and the outlier among the five bodies checked. Brookings separately identifies Tax Foundation as an outlier in the TCJA dynamic-scoring context. Label the lean.

feedback.selfFinanceQuote: tax cuts rarely if ever fully pay for themselves. Because taxes capture only a fraction of income and some spending grows with income, a policy would need to produce $5 to $6 of economic activity for every $1 of cost to be self-financing.
feedback.neverClaim: No lever combination in the tool may ever display a rate cut with net-positive revenue. This is gameplan §9 test 7.

params.lesson: Conventional scores agree within roughly plus or minus 20 percent. Dynamic scores diverge by a factor of about four for the identical bill — driven overwhelmingly by ONE assumption: whether deficit-financed cuts crowd out private investment. That is why the model-lens toggle is a first-class UI feature and not a settings-menu afterthought.

payroll.ssaSrc: SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, provisions summary, 2025 Trustees Report basis
payroll.loadBearing: THE 'HALF TO TWO-THIRDS' RANGE IS NOT UNCERTAINTY — IT IS A POLICY CHOICE. Crediting the new earnings toward benefits drops the shortfall closed from 67% (E2.1) to 48% (E2.2). The tool MUST state which variant it means. This is a perfect why-panel: the same headline policy produces two very different answers depending on one design decision nobody talks about.

enforcement.auditSrc: Boning, Hendren, Sprung-Keyser & Stuart, NBER w31376 / QJE 2025
enforcement.auditCaveat: The dossier attributed this to the wrong paper number. It is w31376. Also note the ROI is contested and falls as funding scales — a caveat the tool must carry per the dossier's own instruction.
visibility: Little or no info reporting (self-employment, pass-through)
enforcement.contested: Funding the IRS is one of the only levers in the tool where $1 in reliably returns more than $1 out. It is also the only near-free-lunch item, which is exactly why it needs the contested-ROI caveat attached — a tool that presents one free lunch without a caveat has undermined its own credibility on everything else.

capGains.the_spread_is_the_finding: For a ~4-5pp increase, PWBM says ~$66B/10yr while Agersnap & Zidar imply ~$180-300B/10yr — a 3-5x SPREAD driven entirely by realization-elasticity assumptions. Tax Foundation's $362.5B for a 10pp increase sits between them and is notably SUBLINEAR, consistent with a high elasticity. There is no consensus number. The engine must produce a RANGE here, and if it produces a point estimate the guardrail test has failed.

estimates.note: BEST AVAILABLE and on the correct baseline. No CBO, JCT, or TPC standalone post-OBBBA 199A repeal score exists.
A different policy. Do not use as a repeal benchmark.

seventy.note: Gameplan §4 Act 3 item 2 calls for showing 70%-alone versus 70%-paired-with-capital-gains as a deliberate contrast. The data now supports that precisely: $291.7B conventional standing alone, versus $51.4B conventional / -$63.5B dynamic once gains are included. Most top-0.05% income is capital gains, which an ordinary-rate lever does not touch — that is the realization doctrine in one comparison.
seventy.groupDef: DOLLAR BAND — taxable income above $10 million. NOT a percentile.
drivers: WHETHER THE 70% RATE APPLIES TO CAPITAL GAINS. Including gains flips Tax Foundation's dynamic score NEGATIVE (-$63.5B), because realizations collapse. This is the single most instructive number on the card.
WHETHER PASS-THROUGH OWNERS REINCORPORATE AS C CORPORATIONS. PWBM finds a 73.8% net pass-through rate vs 39.8% for C corps — 'the largest tax wedge in recent U.S. history.'
